title: From Tube to Vitamin K: Citrate Specimen Rules, Factor VII and Correction Timing
summary: Learn the citrate specimen rules that keep PT and APTT honest, why factor VII’s short half-life makes an isolated long PT the first sign of vitamin K deficiency or warfarin effect, and why vitamin K needs hours while prothrombin complex concentrate acts at once.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 36 Hit 7 (factor half-lives), Hit 13 (specimen rules) and Trap 5 (vitamin K timing). Checked against Magnette 2016, Castaman & Linari 2017, Vigué 2009, Mathews & Hayward 2025 and Witt 2016. Hit 13 says freeze platelet-free plasma at −20 °C and that holding over 4 hours lowers FVIII/VWF; Magnette 2016 prefers −70 °C or below (−20 °C keeps most tests about 2 weeks), keeps PT/INR stable about 24 h, and links low VWF to cold storage (VWF stable 48 h at room temperature) (register flag rv-ch36-coag-specimen-storage). Trap 5 says vitamin K “must be given IV”; Witt 2016 prefers oral vitamin K without major bleeding and reserves slow IV plus PCC for major bleeding (register flag rv-ch36-vitk-route). Hit 7 gives FVII 3–6 h; sources read give about 3–4 h (Castaman) and 4.2 h (PCC study quoted by Vigué). Not taught: FVIII/FIX recovery per IU/kg, EHL products, paediatric half-life shortening, the 25–50 mL saline volume and the 15-minute lower infusion bound.

objectives: Apply citrate specimen rules: tube, fill, temperature, time limits and freezing.
Explain why factor VII’s short half-life makes an isolated prolonged PT the earliest sign of vitamin K deficiency or warfarin effect.
Describe the timing and route of vitamin K correction and when prothrombin complex concentrate is added.

scenes.title: Three long clotting times
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three coagulation puzzles arrive on one shift — (1) a citrate tube for PT and APTT that sat on the bench for 6 hours before testing, now showing a long APTT; (2) an outpatient on no medication with an isolated prolonged PT and a normal APTT; (3) a warfarin patient with a major bleed who has just received intravenous vitamin K, and the team asks for a repeat INR in 15 minutes. Question token: “Specimen, biology, or timing?”

cues.text: Three long clotting times arrive on one shift. First, a citrate tube that sat on the bench for six hours, now with a long APTT.
Second, an isolated prolonged PT with a normal APTT. Third, a bleeding warfarin patient just given intravenous vitamin K, with a repeat INR ordered in fifteen minutes.
Is each problem the specimen, the biology, or the timing?

scenes.title: A clotting time starts in the tube
scenes.altText: Schematic: four cards on the citrate specimen (Magnette 2016 summary of CLSI and other guidance). Tube: sodium citrate 105–109 mmol/L (3.2%), filled to at least 90% of nominal volume, giving the required 1 part citrate to 9 parts blood. Transport and hold: room temperature (15–25 °C); cold storage of whole blood can drop factor VIII and von Willebrand factor below the reference range and mimic haemophilia A or von Willebrand disease. Time limits: PT/INR samples are stable about 24 hours at room temperature; APTT within 4 hours on fresh plasma (labile factor VIII and possibly factor V); APTT for unfractionated heparin: centrifuge within 1 hour. Freezing: double centrifugation to platelet-poor plasma with residual platelets ≤10 × 10⁹/L; store preferably at −70 °C or below; −20 °C keeps most parameters only about 2 weeks; ship frozen aliquots on dry ice.

cues.text: A clotting time starts in the tube. Use 3.2 percent sodium citrate and fill the tube to at least ninety percent, so the ratio is one part citrate to nine parts blood. An underfilled tube has too much citrate and lengthens clotting times.
Keep the sample at room temperature. Putting whole blood on ice or in the fridge can drop factor eight and von Willebrand factor, and falsely suggest haemophilia A or von Willebrand disease.

Time limits differ by test. PT and INR samples are stable for about twenty-four hours, but the APTT should be run within four hours, because factor eight and possibly factor five decay. A heparin APTT sample should be spun within one hour.
Plasma that must be frozen is spun twice, to fewer than ten billion platelets per litre. Freeze at minus seventy or colder; minus twenty keeps most tests for only about two weeks.

scenes.title: Factor VII is first to fall
scenes.altText: Schematic half-life ladder (Castaman 2017 table of plasma half-lives; Vigué 2009 quoting a PCC pharmacokinetic study): factor VII about 3–4 hours (shortest); factor VIII 10–12 hours; factor X 40–60 hours; prothrombin (factor II) 3–4 days; factor XIII 11–14 days (longest). Card: vitamin K–dependent proteins are factors II, VII, IX and X plus the anticoagulant proteins C, S and Z. Card: in vitamin K deficiency or early vitamin K antagonist effect, factor VII falls first, so the PT/INR can be prolonged alone before falling II, IX and X lengthen the APTT (Mathews & Hayward 2025). Protein C also has a short half-life, similar to factor VII.

cues.text: Now the biology. Clotting factors are made and cleared at different speeds. Factor seven has the shortest half-life, about three to four hours. Factor thirteen has the longest, about eleven to fourteen days.
Vitamin K is needed to make factors two, seven, nine and ten, and the anticoagulant proteins C, S and Z.
When vitamin K action stops, from deficiency or warfarin, factor seven runs out first. So the PT and INR can lengthen on their own, before falling factors two, nine and ten prolong the APTT.

That is the hook’s second case: an isolated prolonged PT points to factor seven, either an inherited deficiency or early vitamin K deficiency. Protein C also falls fast, with a half-life similar to factor seven.

props.title: Vitamin K action stops
lines: Then II, IX, X: APTT too

props.label: Isolated long PT → think factor VII first

scenes.title: Vitamin K needs hours
scenes.altText: Timing cards. Vitamin K alone is slow: the liver must synthesise new carboxylated factors. After intravenous vitamin K the INR starts to fall within about 4 hours, but that early fall is mostly a rise in factor VII and can mislead (Vigué 2009); coagulopathy typically improves within a few hours, and a second 10 mg IV dose 12 hours later prevents a rebound INR (Mathews & Hayward 2025). Route card: IV vitamin K is given as a slow infusion (about 30 minutes in Mathews & Hayward) because of a small anaphylaxis risk; for major warfarin bleeding, 5–10 mg slow IV plus four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) for immediate factor replacement; without major bleeding, oral vitamin K is preferred; subcutaneous absorption is unpredictable (Witt 2016). Diagnostic card: a prolonged PT/INR that corrects after vitamin K supports vitamin K deficiency. Hook answers: (1) recollect, APTT past 4 hours; (2) think factor VII; (3) a 15-minute INR after vitamin K is too early; PCC gives the immediate correction.

cues.text: Vitamin K does not add clotting factors; the liver must build them. After an intravenous dose, the INR starts to fall within about four hours, but that early fall is mostly factor seven, so it can overstate recovery.

For a major warfarin bleed, give five to ten milligrams intravenously, slowly, because of a small anaphylaxis risk, together with prothrombin complex concentrate, which replaces factors at once. Without major bleeding, oral vitamin K is preferred.
A prolonged PT that corrects after vitamin K also supports a diagnosis of vitamin K deficiency.

Back to the hook. Case one: recollect, because the APTT is past four hours. Case two: think factor seven. Case three: an INR fifteen minutes after vitamin K is far too early; the concentrate gives the fast correction.

props.label: Corrects after vitamin K → VK deficiency

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Vitamin K works immediately — recheck in 15 minutes” (✓ it needs hours of new factor synthesis; the early INR fall is mostly factor VII; PCC gives immediate replacement); “Chill the coagulation tube to protect it” (✓ hold whole blood at room temperature; cold lowers factor VIII and VWF); “An isolated long PT means haemophilia” (✓ haemophilia A and B prolong the APTT; an isolated long PT points to factor VII).

cues.text: Trap one: vitamin K works immediately. No: it needs hours of new factor synthesis. For speed, prothrombin complex concentrate is added.
Trap two: chill the coagulation tube to protect it. No: keep whole blood at room temperature; cold lowers factor eight and von Willebrand factor.
Trap three: an isolated long PT means haemophilia. No: haemophilia prolongs the APTT. An isolated long PT points to factor seven.

scenes.title: Seven is the canary
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Factor VII is the canary in the coal mine: with the shortest half-life it is the first to fall when vitamin K action stops and the first to come back when vitamin K is given — so the PT/INR moves early in both directions. Factor XIII is the tortoise.” Tokens: canary = FVII · first down, first up · tortoise = FXIII. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: factor seven is the canary. With the shortest half-life, it is the first to fall when vitamin K action stops, and the first to return when vitamin K is given, so the INR moves early both ways. Factor thirteen is the tortoise.

Where it breaks: an early INR rise or fall mostly reflects factor seven, while factors two, nine and ten lag, so the INR can overstate recovery; a long PT also has specimen causes; and half-life values vary between sources.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Early INR change is mostly FVII; II, IX, X lag
A long PT can be a specimen problem

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “3.2% citrate · fill ≥90% · room temperature · APTT ≤4 h · freeze ≤ −70 °C”, “FVII shortest half-life → isolated long PT · vitamin K needs hours → PCC for speed”.

cues.text: Keep citrate samples at room temperature and run the APTT within four hours, read an isolated long PT as factor VII first because it has the shortest half-life, and remember that vitamin K needs hours of new factor synthesis, so a major bleed also needs prothrombin complex concentrate.

props.label: 3.2% citrate · fill ≥ 90% · room temp · APTT ≤ 4 h · freeze ≤ −70 °C

explanation.what: Plain language: a clotting time can be wrong because of the tube, and right but surprising because of biology. Factor VII disappears fastest, so it shows trouble first, and vitamin K only works once the liver has made new factors, which takes hours. Scientific terms: 3.2% (105–109 mmol/L) sodium citrate, 1:9 citrate-to-blood ratio, labile factors (FV, FVIII), platelet-poor plasma, double centrifugation, plasma half-life, vitamin K–dependent γ-carboxylation (factors II, VII, IX, X; proteins C, S, Z), prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC).
explanation.why: Underfilling adds excess citrate and lengthens clotting times; cold storage lowers FVIII and VWF; delay lets labile FVIII decay, lengthening the APTT. When vitamin K–dependent carboxylation stops, the factor with the shortest half-life (FVII) falls first, so the PT/INR prolongs before the APTT. Vitamin K restores synthesis, so correction waits on the liver; PCC supplies the factors directly.
explanation.measure: Fill ≥90% (1:9); hold at 15–25 °C; PT/INR stable ~24 h; APTT within 4 h (UFH APTT: centrifuge within 1 h); platelet-poor plasma ≤10 × 10⁹/L platelets for freezing, ≤ −70 °C preferred, −20 °C about 2 weeks. Half-lives: FVII ~3–4 h, FX 40–60 h, FII 3–4 days, FXIII 11–14 days. IV vitamin K: INR falls within ~4 h (mostly FVII); major bleed 5–10 mg slow IV plus PCC; non-bleeding high INR: oral vitamin K preferred.
explanation.differs: Specimen artefact (fill, temperature, delay) vs true factor deficiency; isolated long PT (FVII) vs isolated long APTT (VIII, IX, XI); vitamin K (hours, new synthesis) vs PCC (immediate factor replacement).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: a delayed or chilled sample with a long APTT or low FVIII (recollect), which factor falls first on warfarin or in vitamin K deficiency, and whether vitamin K or PCC gives immediate correction.

questions.stem: A citrate tube for PT and APTT (patient not on heparin) is tested 6 hours after collection after sitting at room temperature. The PT is normal; the APTT is prolonged. What is the best action?

options.text: Request a new specimen and test the APTT within 4 hours
options.rationale: Correct. APTT samples should be tested on fresh plasma within 4 hours; labile factor VIII (and possibly V) decays, lengthening the APTT.

options.text: Report the APTT with a delay comment
options.rationale: Incorrect. The delay can produce a falsely long APTT; a comment does not make the result valid.

options.text: Refrigerate the tube and test it tomorrow
options.rationale: Incorrect. Further delay worsens factor loss, and cold storage of whole blood lowers FVIII and VWF.

options.text: Start a 1:1 mixing study on this specimen
options.rationale: Incorrect. Investigating an APTT from an unsuitable specimen can lead to a false diagnosis; recollect first.

questions.stem: Early in vitamin K deficiency, the PT/INR is prolonged while the APTT is still normal. Which factor explains this pattern?

options.text: Factor VII, which has the shortest half-life
options.rationale: Correct. FVII (about 3–4 hours) falls first, prolonging the PT before II, IX and X fall enough to lengthen the APTT.
Incorrect. Prothrombin has a long half-life (days) and is in both the PT and APTT pathways.
Incorrect. FIX is vitamin K–dependent but is measured by the APTT, not the PT.
Incorrect. FXIII is not vitamin K–dependent, has the longest half-life, and does not affect the PT or APTT.

questions.stem: A patient on warfarin has a major bleed with an INR of 6. Which plan matches the guidance?

options.text: Slow IV vitamin K 5–10 mg plus prothrombin complex concentrate
options.rationale: Correct. Vitamin K restores factor synthesis over hours; PCC replaces factors immediately.

options.text: IV vitamin K alone, then repeat the INR in 15 minutes to confirm correction
options.rationale: Incorrect. Vitamin K needs hours of new hepatic synthesis; a 15-minute INR is too early.

options.text: Subcutaneous vitamin K for the fastest effect
options.rationale: Incorrect. Subcutaneous absorption is unpredictable and is a last resort.

options.text: Rapid IV push of vitamin K to shorten onset
options.rationale: Incorrect. IV vitamin K is given slowly because of a small anaphylaxis risk; speed of injection does not remove the synthesis delay.

claims.text: Citrate concentration, fill and ratio; room-temperature handling and cold-induced FVIII/VWF loss; PT/INR 24 h vs APTT 4 h vs UFH APTT 1 h; platelet-poor plasma for freezing; −70 °C preferred, −20 °C about 2 weeks.
FVII has the shortest plasma half-life (about 3–4 h) and FXIII the longest (11–14 days); FX, FII and FVIII values.
claims.note: The reviewer’s 3–6 h for FVII is wider than the 3–4 h and 4.2 h in the sources read; the lesson teaches about 3–4 h.

claims.text: Vitamin K–dependent proteins; FVII falls first so an isolated long PT/INR can precede APTT prolongation; protein C short half-life; correction after vitamin K supports the diagnosis.
Vitamin K acts through new synthesis; INR falls within about 4 h, mostly FVII; slow IV infusion for anaphylaxis risk; PCC gives immediate factor replacement.
Oral vitamin K preferred without major bleeding; subcutaneous unpredictable; major bleed 5–10 mg slow IV plus four-factor PCC.
FVIII/FIX recovery per IU/kg; EHL half-lives; paediatric half-life shortening; vitamin K in 25–50 mL saline over 15–30 minutes; onset 2–4 h as a fixed range.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 36 Hit 13 says to freeze platelet-free plasma at −20 °C, applies a 4-hour limit to all testing, and links holding over 4 hours to low VWF. Magnette 2016 prefers storage at −70 °C or below (−20 °C keeps most parameters about 2 weeks), gives PT/INR about 24 h stability, and links low FVIII/VWF to cold storage while VWF is stable 48 h at room temperature (register flag rv-ch36-coag-specimen-storage).

Ch. 36 Trap 5 says vitamin K “must be given IV slowly”. Witt 2016 prefers oral vitamin K for non-bleeding patients with a high INR and reserves slow IV vitamin K (with four-factor PCC) for major bleeding (register flag rv-ch36-vitk-route).
